metadata.title: Prominent Washington lawyer Tom Goldstein convicted at tax trial

left: On Feb 25, a 12-person jury in Greenbelt, Maryland convicted Thomas Goldstein of tax and financial crimes after a seven-week trial, finding him guilty on 12 of the 16 counts he faced.

sources.text:
Tom Goldstein took plenty of losses in his day job as a Supreme Court lawyer, including being on the wrong side of the Bush v. Gore decision. He’s learned even more about losing from his side hustle. For over 20 years, Goldstein has been an avid poker player with a weakness for playing aggressively with big pots of money. He has lost money in livestreamed games and at the table with celebrities, including $200,000 at Kevin Hart’s birthday party in Mykonos two summers back.
But on Wednesday afternoon, Goldstein, 56, suffered the biggest loss of his career when a jury convicted him in federal court on 12 of 16 charges related to tax and mortgage fraud. After three days of deliberating, the jury found him guilty on charges including tax evasion, making a false statement on a loan application, and aiding and assisting in preparation of a false tax return. It was all related to his yearslong scheme to hide his poker winnings from his wife, his law firm, mortgage lenders, and the Internal Revenue Service. This concealed second life was only fully understood after he was charged last year.
“For those of us who are his friends and supporters, this is the verdict we’ve been dreading,” says a friend following the trial. “I thought Tom had a pretty good defense — claiming that the mistakes on his tax filings were by his accountant and that they were unintentional. But it was a bit of a long shot.”
During the seven-week trial, Goldstein and his legal team — led by Jonathan Kravis of the white-shoe firm Munger, Tolles & Olsen — argued that the millions of dollars of poker winnings he did not disclose on time were a series of errors by him and his accountant. “The mistakes, responsibility for those tax years is mine,” he said on the stand. “It’s just very different from whether I committed a crime.”
Prosecutors argued that the jury should consider just who was behind the defendant’s bench. “Mr. Goldstein is probably the smartest person in this courtroom,” Justice Department senior-litigation counsel Sean Beaty told the jury. Not only had Goldstein personally argued 45 cases before the Supreme Court, he had also fundamentally changed how lawyers even get cases in front of the court, taught at Harvard and Stanford, and founded the influential SCOTUSblog, which law nerds read religiously to parse landmark decisions.
The prosecution cited evidence of Goldstein lying to IRS agents and hiding his debts from his accountants and mortgage lenders, including his failure to disclose a $15 million gambling debt on a mortgage application on his home in Washington, D.C, in 2021. “Smart people generally don’t document their tax evasion,” Beaty told jurors. “They hide it in the tall grass. The crime here is the concealment.”
Goldstein’s decision to hide his life as a prolific poker player in Las Vegas and Macau could have hurt him on charges that rely on intent. Tax-fraud charges demand that prosecutors prove a defendant willingly knew they broke the law and that it wasn’t just an accident. By spending years concealing his high-stakes poker lifestyle from his family and his law firm, Goldstein made it so the government was able “to paint a picture and show the jury that he lied to everybody,” says a former mentee and friend. “That is circumstantial, inferential evidence of intent that speaks to the defendant’s state of mind. In tax cases, when a defendant lies to everyone, they are more likely to be convicted.”
This friend was also struck by a PR move just before the trial, when Goldstein sat down with Jeffrey Toobin for a tell-all in The New York Times Magazine. It wasn’t the scandalous details that painted the bookish-looking attorney as a Scorsese character living it up before a fall from grace. (The profile describes how Goldstein brought four of his girlfriends on vacation to Costa Rica and paid the rent for three of them — whom he was seeing at the same time — to live in the same house in California.) It was the moment in which Goldstein brought Toobin to his home office and told him to “look at anything you like,” offering a peek at his tax returns, bank records, and other files turned over during discovery. “I have never, ever believed that I did anything wrong,” he says to Toobin.
“The way I read the Toobin interview is that Tom convinced himself by saying over and over that he had a strong case and didn’t do anything wrong,” the friend says. “But the evidence suggests otherwise. And the jury found otherwise.”
Evidence presented at trial also provided a look into the world of elite private poker. Tobey Maguire, a serious player dating back to the Molly’s Game era, testified for the prosecution, stating that he hired Goldstein to collect $7 million in winnings from the Texas billionaire Andy Beal. (Goldstein then diverted his $50,000 fee to a lender to pay off his gambling debts, according to prosecutors.) In total, prosecutors claim that Goldstein won $50 million playing one-on-one poker matches dating back to 2014. He was notorious for playing recklessly, with several opponents documenting his habit of betting without even looking at his cards. “I may have overcooked it a little bit,” he said on the stand. (Goldstein’s attorney did not respond to a request for comment.)
Another legal friend who has known Goldstein for 30 years was furious over the 12 guilty counts. “Yes, he fucked up and failed to report his income some years, but he showed that he grotesquely overreported in other years,” says the friend, who attended several days of the trial, including the first day of Goldstein’s testimony. “Tom is a very calm guy, and that plays great at the Supreme Court and with other lawyers,” he says. “You see the logic of his arguments. He doesn’t yell and scream. But I don’t know how well that connects with a jury. He was so calm about it you wonder if the jury thinks that he’s some calculated dude rather than a guy who just fucked up and is getting overly punished for it.” (He did not mince words about his feelings toward the prosecution: “The guy who cross-examined Tom reminded me of every big frat boy I’ve ever met — they’re just assholes.”)
Around the time of the trial, this friend was also in touch with Goldstein. “He’s highly stressed,” he says. “Not just of the risk of going to jail. There are lots of other aspects of his life that are blowing up.” He said that while Goldstein’s father and stepmother were in attendance on the first day of his testimony, his wife, Amy Howe, was not there. Howe remains the “primary reporter” at SCOTUSblog, which was sold just after Goldstein’s indictment. But she has not spoken to the press on her husband’s legal trouble. In his profile, Toobin wrote only that their “marriage of three decades is ending.” Goldstein once said that Howe was the only reason he made it through law school. On the morning of her husband’s conviction, she moderated the SCOTUSblog chat as the opinions for Villarreal v. Texas and The GEO Group, Inc. v. Menocal were made public.
In 2023, as the Feds were investigating him, Goldstein stepped down from his law firm and his Supreme Court work. In the coming months, he is likely to be disbarred. The judge on the case, Lydia Kay Griggsby, has yet to announce a sentencing date, though friends expect Goldstein will appeal. But white-collar defense attorney and former federal prosecutor Robert Stahl expects that he could face years in prison. “A judge is going to look at Goldstein’s background and knowledge of tax laws,” he says. “My experience is that lawyers are held to a higher standard because of the oath to uphold the laws of the Constitution.” Goldstein and Howe are facing another problem in the coming weeks. Late last year, prosecutors barred the sale of Goldstein’s home in D.C. to pay for his legal bills, because it was the property he lied about on a mortgage application. The government now intends to seize the $3 million house.

A top Supreme Court litigator and co-founder of the website SCOTUSblog was convicted by a federal jury after being charged with failing to pay taxes on millions of dollars in gambling income stemming from his lifestyle as an ultra-high-stakes poker player.
Thomas Goldstein, who once was part of the legal team that represented Al Gore in the Supreme Court litigation over the 2000 election ultimately won by George W. Bush, was found guilty of 12 of 16 counts on Wednesday following a six-week trial in Maryland.
"He lied to everyone around him," Justice Department prosecutor Sean Beaty said during the trial’s closing arguments.
"It was a textbook tax-evasion scheme," Beaty added. "And Mr. Goldstein executed that nearly flawlessly."
Jurors deliberated for approximately two days before convicting Goldstein of one count of tax evasion, four of eight counts of aiding and assisting in the preparation of false tax returns, four counts of willful failure to timely pay taxes and three counts of false statements on loan applications.
Justice Department prosecutors also accused him of diverting money from his law firm to pay gambling debts and falsely deducting gambling debts as business expenses.
Goldstein argued more than 40 cases before the Supreme Court before retiring in 2023.
His defense attorney, Jonathan Kravis, told jurors that Goldstein made "innocent mistakes" on his tax returns but didn’t cheat on his taxes or knowingly make false statements on his tax returns, according to The Associated Press.
"A mistake is not a crime," Kravis said, claiming the government rushed to judgment and failed to adequately investigate the case.
Goldstein raked in approximately $50 million in poker winnings in 2016, including roughly $22 million that he won playing in Asia, according to Beaty. The prosecutor said the tax evasion scheme "fell apart" when another gambler, feeling cheated by Goldstein, notified the IRS about a 2016 debt owed to the attorney.

Goldstein, who testified in his own defense, denied any wrongdoing. He has said he repeatedly instructed his law firm’s staff and accountants to correctly characterize his personal expenses.

Supreme Court litigator convicted of tax evasion over income from high-stakes poker
WASHINGTON (AP) — A prominent Supreme Court litigator who also published a popular blog about the nation’s highest court was convicted Wednesday of tax evasion and related charges stemming from his secretive lifestyle as an ultra-high-stakes poker player.
A federal jury found SCOTUSblog co-founder Thomas Goldstein guilty of 12 of 16 counts after a six-week trial in Greenbelt, Maryland. Jurors deliberated for approximately two days before convicting Goldstein of one count of tax evasion, four of eight counts of aiding and assisting in the preparation of false tax returns, four counts of willful failure to timely pay taxes, and three counts of false statements on loan applications.
Goldstein was charged with failing to pay taxes on millions of dollars in gambling income. Justice Department prosecutors also accused him of diverting money from his law firm to pay gambling debts and falsely deducting gambling debts as business expenses.
Goldstein argued more than 40 cases before the Supreme Court before retiring in 2023. He was part of the legal team that represented Democrat Al Gore in the Supreme Court litigation over the 2000 election ultimately won by Republican President George W. Bush.
Goldstein’s indictment a year ago sent shockwaves through the legal community in Washington, D.C. Many friends and colleagues didn’t know the extent of his gambling.
“He lied to everyone around him,” Justice Department prosecutor Sean Beaty said during the trial’s closing arguments.
Defense attorney Jonathan Kravis said the government rushed to judgment and failed to adequately investigate the case. Goldstein made “innocent mistakes” on his tax returns but didn’t cheat on his taxes or knowingly make false statements on his tax returns, Kravis told jurors.
“A mistake is not a crime,” he said.
Beaty described Goldstein as a “willful tax cheat.” Goldstein raked in approximately $50 million in poker winnings in 2016, including roughly $22 million that he won playing in Asia, according to Beaty. The prosecutor said the tax evasion scheme “fell apart” when another gambler, feeling cheated by Goldstein, notified the IRS about a 2016 debt owed to the attorney.
“It was a textbook tax-evasion scheme,” Beaty said. “And Mr. Goldstein executed that nearly flawlessly.”
The trial, which started Jan. 12, included testimony by “Spider-Man” star Tobey Maguire, an avid poker player who enlisted Goldstein’s help in recovering a gambling debt from a billionaire.
Goldstein, who testified in his own defense, denied any wrongdoing. He has said he repeatedly instructed his law firm’s staff and accountants to correctly characterize his personal expenses. In a 2014 email, he told a firm employee that “we always play completely by the rules.”
Goldstein also was accused of lying to IRS agents and hiding his gambling debts from his accountants, employees and mortgage lenders. He omitted a $15 million gambling debt from mortgage loan applications while looking for a new home in Washington, D.C., with his wife in 2021, his indictment alleges.
“He was thinking only of his wife when he left off the gambling debts,” Kravis said.
